title: The Shattered Jar at Topheth
summary: God tells Jeremiah to buy a clay jar, take elders and senior priests to the Valley of Ben-hinnom, and announce there a disaster that will make ears ring, because Judah has filled the place with the blood of children burned to Baal. Before the witnesses he smashes the jar, declaring that God will shatter the city in the same way, beyond repair. Then he repeats the message in the temple courtyard to all the people.
story: In chapter 18 Jeremiah watched soft clay being reshaped, a picture of a people who could still turn. In chapter 19 the clay has been fired. A finished jar cannot be remade, only broken, and the prophet breaks it. The move from the potter's wheel to the smashed jar marks a turning point in the book: the invitation of chapter 18 has been refused, and the judgment now announced is final for this generation. The public setting (the valley, the elders, the temple court) also sets off the confrontation that follows immediately in chapter 20, when the priest in charge of the temple has Jeremiah beaten.
historical:
The Valley of Ben-hinnom (the valley of the son of Hinnom) runs along the west and south sides of ancient Jerusalem and meets the Kidron Valley south of the city. In it lay Topheth, a place of child sacrifice. The books of Kings record that King Ahaz and later King Manasseh made their sons pass through the fire (2 Kings 16:3; 21:6), and that Josiah, as part of his reform around 622 BC, defiled Topheth so that no one could burn a son or daughter there to Molech (2 Kings 23:10). Jeremiah's preaching shows that the practice or its memory had returned after Josiah's death. Here the sacrifices are said to be offered to Baal; in 7:31 and 32:35 the same valley is connected with Molech. Scholars debate whether Molech was a distinct god, a title, or the name of a kind of sacrifice, but the texts are clear that children were killed.

The Potsherd Gate (verse 2) opened toward the valley; its exact location is unknown, but its name suggests it was where broken pottery was thrown out, a fitting spot to shatter a jar. The siege horrors of verse 9 recall the covenant curses of Deuteronomy 28:53-57, and Lamentations records that they took place when Babylon besieged Jerusalem in 588 to 586 BC (Lamentations 2:20; 4:10).
cultural:
Child sacrifice was known in the ancient Mediterranean and Near East, especially in times of crisis, as a supreme offering to secure a god's help (2 Kings 3:27 describes the king of Moab sacrificing his son on the city wall during a siege). Israel's law forbade it absolutely (Leviticus 18:21; Deuteronomy 12:31; 18:10). The phrase in verse 5, "something I never commanded or mentioned, nor did it even enter My mind", may answer people who thought they were giving God the costliest gift possible, perhaps by misreading the law that the firstborn belonged to the LORD. God says it is utterly foreign to him.

The jar (verse 1) was an earthenware flask with a narrow neck, and some interpreters think its Hebrew name imitates the gurgling sound of liquid being poured from it. Smashing pottery could carry meaning in the ancient world; Egyptian execration texts, for instance, wrote the names of enemies on bowls or figurines that were then broken to curse them. The rooftop worship of verse 13 reflects a real practice: flat roofs were used for daily life, and incense and drink offerings were burned there to the sun, moon, and stars (the "host of heaven"), practices Josiah had also tried to end (2 Kings 23:12; Zephaniah 1:5).
literary: This is a sign-act in two scenes. Verses 1 to 13 give God's instructions, a long speech Jeremiah is to proclaim in the valley, and the command to break the jar with its meaning. The speech plays on the place: Topheth will be renamed "the Valley of Slaughter", the city itself will become "like Topheth", and the place of burning will become a place of burial with no room left. The word "place" occurs eight times, tying the judgment to the site of the sin. Verses 14 and 15 are a brief narrative in which Jeremiah repeats the message at the temple, which leads directly into the next chapter. The Hebrew contains a sound play in verse 7: God will "ruin" (baqqoti) the plans of Judah, echoing the word for the flask (baqbuq), as if God were emptying out the city's plans as one pours out a jar.

outline.t: Buy a jar and go to the Valley of Ben-hinnom
Children burned to Baal: the Valley of Slaughter
The message repeated in the temple courtyard

doctrines.note: Idolatry here reaches its end point: the sacrifice of children. False worship does not only dishonor God; it demands the lives of the vulnerable. The chapter shows that what a people worships eventually shapes what it will do to its own.

The image of a jar that "can never again be repaired" expresses the finality of judgment on this generation. Yet the rest of Jeremiah shows God rebuilding a people after the breaking, so final for them is not final for his purposes.
God declares that child sacrifice never entered his mind. His holiness is not only separateness from sin but the complete opposite of the gods who feed on human lives.

words.note: Topheth, the place of child sacrifice in the Valley of Ben-hinnom. The origin of the name is uncertain; many scholars connect it with a word for a fireplace or hearth, and the Hebrew vowels may have been changed to echo boshet, shame, as happened with some other names of false gods. Its valley, Ge-Hinnom, gave its name (through the Greek Gehenna) to the New Testament's word for the place of final judgment.

Baqbuq, a flask or jug with a narrow neck. Many interpreters think the word imitates the gurgling sound of pouring. It was an everyday household item, which made the sign vivid: Jerusalem, for all its pride, was as breakable as a cheap jar bought from a potter.

Rapha, to heal or repair. In verse 11 the jar "can never again be repaired", literally healed. The same verb runs through Jeremiah's laments over his people's incurable wound (8:22; 15:18) and through God's promise of healing in 30:17 and 33:6. Here the door of healing is closed for the generation that refused it.

christ: Matthew 27:9-10 connects the purchase of the potter's field with Judas's thirty pieces of silver and attributes the prophecy to Jeremiah. The words Matthew cites are closest to Zechariah 11:12-13, and many interpreters think he combined Zechariah with Jeremiah's potter passages (chapters 18 and 19, and the field purchase of chapter 32), naming the more prominent prophet. This chapter's setting, a potter, a valley of death, and innocent blood, supplies part of that picture. The valley itself became, as Gehenna, the image Jesus used most often for final judgment (Mark 9:43-48). And the chapter's horror at the sacrifice of children stands in sharpest contrast to the gospel: where false gods demanded that people give up their children to them, the God of Israel gave his own Son for the life of the world (John 3:16; Romans 8:32). That is a contrast in the story, not a prediction in this chapter.

hard.q: Verse 9 says God will make people eat their own children. Does God cause such a horror?
hard.a: This is one of the most terrible verses in the Bible, and it describes something that really happened in ancient sieges when food ran out (2 Kings 6:28-29; Lamentations 4:10). The verse speaks in the language of the covenant curses (Leviticus 26:29; Deuteronomy 28:53-57), which warned Israel ahead of time where abandoning God would lead. Most interpreters read God's "I will make them" as his handing the city over to the siege and its consequences, rather than as God directly willing cannibalism; the Hebrew Bible often speaks of God as the cause of what he permits as judgment. There is also a bitter correspondence in the chapter: a people who burned their children to Baal would, under siege, see their children consumed again. The verse is not there to be explained away but to show how terrible the fruit of idolatry and violence becomes, and how seriously God takes the blood of the innocent.

questions: The people of Judah sacrificed their children to gods they hoped would protect them. What do people in our own time sacrifice, including children's welfare, for the sake of security, success, or status?
Chapter 18 showed soft clay that could be reshaped; chapter 19 shows a jar that can only be broken. What does it take for a heart to harden past the point of turning?
God says child sacrifice never entered his mind. How does that shape your picture of what God is like and what he asks of people?
